questions.question_text: An economy operating ON its production possibilities curve can produce more guns only by:
questions.option_b: giving up some butter — an opportunity cost
questions.explanation: On the PPC all resources are employed, so more of one good means less of the other. A point INSIDE allows more of both; shifting the curve requires growth, not a production choice.

questions.question_text: Ana makes 12 loaves or 4 pies/hour; Ben makes 6 loaves or 3 pies. Who has comparative advantage in pies?
questions.option_b: Ben, his opportunity cost (2 loaves/pie) is lower than Ana's (3)
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost per pie: Ana 12/4 = 3 loaves; Ben 6/3 = 2. Ben sacrifices less → comparative advantage despite Ana's absolute advantage. Comparative advantage is about RATIOS.

questions.question_text: Which transaction is included in this year's GDP?
questions.option_b: a new car produced and sold this year
questions.explanation: GDP counts NEW final goods produced this year. Used goods were already counted; stocks are asset swaps; transfer payments produce nothing.

questions.question_text: Nominal GDP rose 6% while the deflator rose 4%. Real GDP grew about:
questions.explanation: Real growth ≈ nominal − inflation = 6% − 4% = 2%. Nominal GDP conflates production with prices; the deflator strips out the price change. Adding (option A) reverses the logic.

questions.question_text: A discouraged worker who stops searching causes the official unemployment rate to:
questions.option_b: fall, since he leaves the labor force and isn't counted
questions.explanation: Unemployment = (jobless AND searching) ÷ labor force. Quitting the search removes him from numerator and labor force — mechanically LOWERING the rate even without improvement.

questions.question_text: An engineer laid off because AI replaced her skills experiences which unemployment?
questions.explanation: A mismatch between worker skills and economic demand = structural. Frictional is ordinary job-searching; cyclical follows the business cycle. Structural persists even in expansions.

questions.question_text: A sharp rise in oil prices shifts SRAS left, producing:
questions.option_a: higher price level, higher real GDP
questions.option_b: lower price level, lower real GDP
questions.option_c: higher price level, lower real GDP — stagflation
questions.option_d: lower price level, higher real GDP
questions.explanation: Supply shocks move price level and output in OPPOSITE directions — the stagflation case. This is the policy dilemma: fighting inflation deepens the recession and vice versa.

questions.question_text: With MPC = 0.8, a $100B increase in government spending raises real GDP by at most:
questions.explanation: Spending multiplier = 1/(1−MPC) = 1/0.2 = 5 → $500B. The TAX-cut multiplier is smaller (MPC/(1−MPC) = 4 → $400B) because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved.

questions.question_text: In a recessionary gap with NO policy, the self-correction mechanism predicts:
questions.option_a: wages fall, shifting SRAS right until output returns to potential
questions.explanation: High unemployment pushes nominal wages down → lower costs → SRAS shifts right → output recovers. Keynes's objection was the SPEED ('in the long run we are all dead'), not the mechanism.

questions.question_text: With a 10% reserve ratio, a new $1,000 deposit can create a MAXIMUM of:
questions.option_d: $10,000 in new loans on top of the deposit
questions.explanation: Money multiplier = 1/0.10 = 10 → total $10,000, of which $9,000 is NEWLY created through lending ($1,000 already existed). Read whether the question wants 'new money' or 'total.'

questions.question_text: To fight a recession, the Fed would most likely:
questions.option_b: buy government bonds, raising reserves and lowering interest rates
questions.explanation: Open-market PURCHASES inject reserves → more lending → lower rates → more spending. The other three CONTRACT the money supply. Mnemonic: the Fed BUYS bonds to BOOST the economy.

questions.question_text: An increase in household saving shifts loanable funds supply right, causing:
questions.option_a: higher real interest rate, less investment
questions.option_b: lower real interest rate, more investment
questions.explanation: More saving = more funds supplied → the price of borrowing (real interest rate) falls → firms invest more. This links thrift today to capital formation tomorrow.

questions.question_text: In the long run, an increase in the money supply primarily causes:
questions.option_c: a proportionally higher price level with output back at potential
questions.explanation: Money neutrality: long-run output is set by resources and technology, so money growth ends up in prices (and via Fisher, HIGHER nominal rates). The short-run boost evaporates as wages adjust — the LRAS is vertical.

questions.question_text: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical because:
questions.option_a: inflation and unemployment always move together
questions.option_b: expectations adjust and unemployment returns to its natural rate at any inflation level
questions.explanation: Workers build expected inflation into wages, undoing the short-run trade-off — unemployment settles at the natural rate regardless of inflation. The LRPC sits at the natural rate, never zero.

questions.question_text: Crowding out occurs when deficit-financed fiscal expansion:
questions.option_a: raises interest rates, reducing private investment
questions.explanation: Government borrowing raises demand for loanable funds → real interest rates rise → some private investment is priced out, partly offsetting the stimulus. Graph it in the loanable funds market.

questions.question_text: If U.S. interest rates rise relative to Europe's, the dollar will most likely:
questions.option_b: appreciate as foreign investors demand dollars for U.S. assets
questions.explanation: Higher returns attract foreign capital → investors BUY dollars → dollar appreciates. Chain: interest rates → capital flows → currency demand. A stronger dollar then makes exports pricier.

questions.question_text: A country running a current account deficit must have a capital/financial account that is:
questions.option_b: in surplus of roughly the same magnitude
questions.explanation: The balance of payments balances: importing more than you export means foreigners hold your assets — recorded as financial-account inflows. CA deficit ≡ KA surplus; two sides of one ledger.

questions.option_b: unemployment insurance payouts rising as layoffs increase
questions.explanation: Automatic stabilizers kick in WITHOUT new legislation — UI and progressive taxes expand deficits in downturns by design. A and D are discretionary fiscal policy; C is monetary policy. 'No vote needed' is the test.
